1042	## 6. Task Breakdown
1043	
1044	Break the PRD into logical, atomic tasks. Each task tagged with the recommended skill.
1045	
1046	**Task sizing:** A task is the right size if it touches 1–3 files in one domain area
1047	and can be verified with a single check. A task is also bounded to a single logical commit
1048	— as a strong default, ~≤400 changed LOC across 1–3 files — because
1049	Sonnet-class implementer models degrade non-linearly beyond that
1050	(per-generation output caps trigger truncation). Split a task if:
1051	
1052	- It spans multiple languages or runtimes (e.g., backend service + frontend client).
1053	- It creates a new DB table AND uses it in domain logic — migration is one task,
1054	  domain model is another.
1055	- It involves both creating a component and writing its tests.
1056	- Its Contract implies more than ~400 changed LOC — split along the Contract's
1057	  file or interface seams.
1058	
1059	Never split an atomic change to satisfy the LOC number — every task must leave
1060	the repo verify-green on its own, so cohesion wins over the numeric target.
1061	
1062	**Dependency ordering** — follow the layer order:
1063	
1064	1. Database migration (schema, RLS, triggers, RPCs)
1065	2. Generated DB types
1066	3. Backend proxy handler (if external API)
1067	4. Domain model (entity, DTO, repository)
1068	5. Domain store (reactive state)
1069	6. UI components (pages, components, layouts)
1070	7. Integration wiring (connecting layers, route setup)
1071	8. Tests (unit + integration per layer)
1072	
1073	**Format each task as:**
1074	
1075	```markdown
1076	### Task N: [Short Title]
1077	
1078	- **Skill:** `skill-name`
1079	- **Bundled:** <one-line origin>
1080	- **Description:** What to implement
1081	- **Inputs:** What must exist before this task starts
1082	- **Outputs:** What this task produces
1083	- **Contract:**
1084	  - **Files:** repo-relative paths to create/edit (mark create vs edit)
1085	  - **Interfaces:** exact function/type/interface signatures + exported symbols this task decides
1086	  - **Call-site edits:** each consumer edit, named as file + symbol (what changes at every call site)
1087	- **Acceptance criteria:** a runnable command whose exit code verifies the task (e.g. `npm run test -- <file>`, `grep -q '<anchor>' <path>`), not prose
1088	```
1089	
1090	The `- **Contract:**` block is **required on every task** — it is the surgical
1091	half of the breakdown that lets a downstream implementer execute to the
1092	planner's interface decisions instead of re-deriving them. The
1093	`- **Acceptance criteria:**` bullet is a **runnable command** (a deterministic
1094	check that exits 0 when the task is done), not a prose description; reserve
1095	prose only for a genuinely subjective criterion.
1096	
1097	The `- **Bundled:**` bullet is **required on every task that originated as a
1098	bundled candidate** under the Objective-item triage rule above — a one-line
1099	origin naming what adjacent item it absorbed (e.g. `- **Bundled:** the
1100	settings-toggle UX addition surfaced during discovery`). Omit the bullet
1101	entirely on tasks that were always part of the requested feature. This is a
1102	**prose contract**, read by humans and by `/flow-pr-review` to understand scope
1103	provenance — it is NEVER machine-parsed; no helper may grow a parser for it.
1104	
1105	**Per-change-type surgical forms.** The `Interfaces:` / `Call-site edits:`
1106	sub-bullets assume callable boundaries. When a task's change type has none,
1107	substitute the change-type-appropriate surgical form — the same Contract slot,
1108	equally exact:
1109	
1110	| Change type    | Surgical form for the Contract block                                                     |
1111	| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
1112	| Code / API     | Exact signatures, exported symbols, and named call-site edits (the default above)        |
1113	| UI / visual    | Exact selectors/components, design tokens, and before → after values per visual property |
1114	| Config / infra | Exact file + key path + before → after values for every key touched                      |
1115	| Docs / prose   | Exact insertion anchor (heading or verbatim phrase) + what is inserted/replaced at it    |
1116	| Schema         | Exact DDL (CREATE/ALTER statements, column types, constraints, policies)                 |

1118	**Strong prior, not a straitjacket.** The Contract block is a strong prior for
1119	the implementer, not a straitjacket: it is authored before any code exists in
1120	the worktree, so a named file, symbol, or signature may be contradicted by the
1121	actual code at implement time. Downstream consumers verify each claim against
1122	the codebase and, on contradiction, prefer the code, adapt, and record the
1123	deviation explicitly (the scout as a `PLAN-DEVIATION:` bullet in its
1124	`## open_questions`; the coder in `rejected_alternatives`) rather than silently
1125	following or silently rewriting the plan. Specify signatures and symbols for
1126	the code the plan _decides_; do not spell out private helper internals — the
1127	depth bound is "enough that the implementer fills in bodies rather than
1128	designing interfaces".

1136	rejected (feedback-loop breakdown, shared-worktree verify gate, the

1204	delta), write the literal word `none` under the heading. Never delete the heading —
1205	`none` is an explicit author affirmation, while a missing heading is ambiguous
1206	between "no change" and "author forgot".>
1207	
1208	## System changes
1209	
1210	<Any internal change worth a reviewer's attention: a subsystem boundary that moved, a
1211	public contract that changed, a performance characteristic, or an ongoing cost. Derive changed-behavior
1212	bullets, in the same parent + `**Before:**` / `**After:**` shape, from plan.md's
1213	`### System flow` subsection when that subsection is non-`none` (a System-flow pair
1214	copied into the PR gains an outcome parent bullet; a top-level `**Before:**` is
1215	flagged), and phrase each deliverable as a capability, not a file
1216	path. When the change moves an ongoing cost — API calls, CI time, token spend — name
1217	the direction and rough size; stay silent about cost when the change does not move one.
1218	
1219	Do not list file edits, helper refactors, or mechanical cleanups. If the change does
1220	not alter a subsystem boundary, a public contract, performance, or ongoing spend,
1221	write `none`.
1222	
1223	Never delete the heading. Exactly like `## User-facing changes` above, `none` is an
1224	explicit author affirmation, while a missing heading is ambiguous between "no change"
1225	and "author forgot".>
1226	
1227	## Why
1228	
1229	<Distill the Problem Statement into 1–3 sentences. Keep the user's pain point and
1230	why it matters — strip solution language. This should read as motivation, not a
1231	feature spec. On a fix-shaped PR — the pipeline exists to fix an observed defect, or
1232	the branch's dominant commit type is `fix:` — lead with `**Failing:**` naming the
1233	observed failure and `**Root cause:**` naming why it happened, before the
1234	1–3-sentence motivation. When step 1.9 resolved a brief, frame the pain in its
1235	ranked priorities and `Use` vocabulary; on `{"found":false}` change nothing.>
1236	
1237	## Key decisions
1238	
1239	<Pull from Architecture Decisions and Scope Boundary's "Out of scope". On a fix-shaped
1240	PR, the FIRST bullet is `**Fix mechanism:** <why the change eliminates the root
1241	cause>`. Each bullet: the decision + a brief rationale. Include scope exclusions
1242	that a reviewer might wonder about. Also list each bundled task (every task
1243	carrying a `- **Bundled:**` bullet in the task breakdown) as its own
1244	`Bundled: <one-line origin>` bullet, so a reviewer can see why the diff is larger
1245	than the requested feature alone.>
1246	
1247	## Instrumentation
1248	
1249	<Omit-when-none — only when the plan's `## Instrumentation` section is not
1250	`none`: the metrics, dashboard panels and alert/SLO spec, distilled from the plan
1251	section per `<SKILL_DIR>/references/discovery-instrumentation.md`. It links the
1252	dashboard URL from `.flow/metrics.md` `## Dashboards` and names the panels the
1253	change adds, or says `spec-only` when no URL exists yet; never a per-panel URL.
1254	Omit the heading entirely when the plan section is `none`.>
1255	
1256	## Deviations from plan
1257	
1258	<Omit-when-empty — authored EMPTY at draft time (the draft omits this
1259	heading entirely). One bullet per meaningful deviation between the
1260	approved plan and what shipped, per
1261	`skills/pipeline/flow-pipeline/references/pause-output-contract.md`
1262	`## Definitions`; `/flow-pr-review` Step 11d populates it post-hoc
1263	from the accuracy sync, never discovery.>
1264	
1265	## Test Steps
1266	
1267	<Verification steps for this PR — both automated and manual smoke. The heading is
1268	also the auto-merge gate signal — see
1269	`skills/pipeline/flow-pipeline/references/auto-merge-rubric.md` for the full
1270	contract. The short version: zero unchecked `- [ ]` items ⇒ auto-merge; one or
1271	more ⇒ gated.
1272	
1273	Always emit the heading. Decide the body based on the PRD:
1274	
1275	- If the PRD describes a pure-internal change (refactor, infra, doc fix,
1276	  generated-code regen) with no user-observable delta — leave the section empty
1277	  under just the placeholder HTML comment. The rubric strips HTML comments before
1278	  counting, so zero unchecked items ⇒ auto-merge.
1279	- Otherwise — populate with `- [ ]` items derived from the acceptance criteria in
1280	  User Stories, applying the **automation test** from
1281	  `skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md` ("Automate first"
1282	  section) to each candidate item _before_ you write it. The test:
1283	
1284	  > Can I name (a) a fixture / setup, (b) one or more deterministic assertions, and
1285	  > (c) an exit condition — all without subjective human judgment? If yes, this is
1286	  > a runnable item, not manual prose.
1287	
1288	  On a fix-shaped PR, include at least one item that names a specific runnable
1289	  regression check (a test file, a fixture, or a reproducible command) that failed
1290	  before the fix and passes after it — not just a generic "tests pass" bullet.
1291	
1292	  When the answer is yes, write the item as the deterministic shell command itself
1293	  (`npm run test -- <file>`, `bun bin/<helper>.test.ts`, `gh pr view <n> --json …
1294	--jq …`, `test -f <path>`, `grep -q <pattern> <file>`,
1295	  `[ "$(cat <path>)" = "<expected>" ]`) so `/flow-pr-review` Step 8c can run it and tick
1296	  the box. Manual prose survives only when the rubric flags the scenario as genuinely
1297	  manual (subjective UX, production-only integrations, cross-browser rendering,
1298	  performance under realistic load). A step whose only unmet preconditions are
1299	  `local and reversible` (start the dev server, bring up / seed the local DB, set a
1300	  local `.env` var, drive a headless browser) is `locally satisfiable` — write it as
1301	  the runnable setup-plus-assertion (perform the setup, then assert), NOT pre-labeled
1302	  "manual — needs the local stack"; see
1303	  `skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md` ("Genuinely manual")
1304	  for the boundary. Use as many items as the change warrants — don't pad to look
1305	  thorough and don't truncate to look concise.
1306	
1307	  When the PRD describes **multiple distinct user-facing behaviors** (several facets,
1308	  commands, or states), emit at least one end-user functional check per distinct change —
1309	  not a single representative step that conflates them — so the checklist shows the full
1310	  scope of new behavior and no facet can break silently because nothing asserted it. This
1311	  is the breadth axis, orthogonal to the happy/unhappy/edge depth categories; each facet
1312	  still routes through the automation test above (automate where automatable, manual only
1313	  where genuinely manual — it is not a mandate to add manual prose). See
1314	  `skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md` ("Coverage breadth") for the
1315	  requirement and a worked multi-facet example.
1316	
1317	  **MUST Read `<SKILL_DIR>/references/discovery-ui.md` before authoring a UI-touching plan's sections or Test Steps.**
1318	
1319	  For whatever stays manual, spell out the exact how for every precondition the step states —
1320	  name the command, click path, or setting that satisfies it, assuming no prior knowledge of
1321	  project-specific toggles or jargon, and never a bare "turn X on" / "with X enabled" without
1322	  the concrete steps. See
1323	  `skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md` ("Precondition concreteness")
1324	  for the rule and a before/after example. Bind each `- [ ]` item to exactly one imperative action,
1325	  matching the rubric's worked example — split an item bundling setup and assertion into two
1326	  boxes; detail rides as an indented sub-bullet or a parenthetical, never a second action on
1327	  the same line; and name the actor when the step is not performed by the reader.
1328	  Test Steps keep the `- [ ]` checkbox form and are NEVER renumbered to ordinals, because the
1329	  auto-merge gate counts unchecked boxes — see
1330	  `skills/pipeline/flow-pipeline/references/pause-output-contract.md` ("Step contract") for the
1331	  shape rule this carve-out belongs to.
1332	
1333	  Human-only items use exactly two labels, a browser behaviour check has one shape, and post-merge
1334	  chores never appear: `SUBJECTIVE: ` is a taste call about rendered UI (review attaches a
1335	  screenshot under it), `DECISION: ` asks the user to accept a named trade-off, a behaviour check
1336	  is written `- [ ] Browser: on <route>, <action> — expect <result>` (one action chain, one
1337	  expected result per box), any clause a second observer would record identically leaves a taste
1338	  item and becomes its own runnable item, and a step that can only be done after merge or deploy
1339	  goes to `flow-followups` instead. See
1340	  `skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md` ("Decision checks",
1341	  "Behaviour checks: the Browser: shape", "Split rule: a taste item holds only taste", "Shallow
1342	  smells") — do not inline the rule bodies.
1343	
1344	  After saving the draft, lint it and fix each finding before moving on (a `suggestion` is a
1345	  judgment call, not a must-fix). Tolerant: when the command is not on PATH, record the named
1346	  skip `test-steps-lint: helper not installed` and continue — never a hard failure:
1347	
1348	  ```bash
1349	  if command -v flow-test-steps-lint >/dev/null; then
1350	    flow-test-steps-lint --body-file .flow-tmp/pr-description-draft.md --phase authoring 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.findings[] | "\(.severity) \(.code) L\(.line): \(.hint)"'
1351	  else
1352	    echo "test-steps-lint: helper not installed"
1353	  fi
1354	  ```
1355	
1356	Open the `## Test Steps` section with this HTML comment, copied verbatim, between
1357	the heading and the first `- [ ]` item. The auto-merge gate strips HTML comments
1358	before counting so the marker is invisible to the count, and any later editor (an
1359	agent re-running pr-review, a human pasting in steps) sees the same standard:
1360	
1361	```html
1362	<!-- flow:authoring-rubric — for each checkbox item below, the three-question
1363	automation test from manual-test-rubric.md is: (a) named fixture/setup,
1364	(b) deterministic assertion(s), (c) exit condition. If all three are answerable
1365	without subjective human judgment, it must be a runnable item. Source of truth:
1366	skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md. -->
1367	```
1368	````
1369	
1370	Example (auto-merge — empty section):
1371	
1372	<!-- No human verification needed — pure-internal change. -->
1373	
1374	Example (gated — non-empty section, marker preserved):
1375	
1376	<!-- flow:authoring-rubric — for each checkbox item below, the three-question
1377	automation test from manual-test-rubric.md is: (a) named fixture/setup,
1378	(b) deterministic assertion(s), (c) exit condition. If all three are answerable
1379	without subjective human judgment, it must be a runnable item. Source of truth:
1380	skills/pipeline/flow-pr-review/references/manual-test-rubric.md. -->
1381	
1382	- [ ] Run `npm run test -- <test-file>` — all specs pass.
1383	- [ ] Run `[ -f <path> ] && grep -q "<expected>" <path>` — config is wired.
1384	- [ ] SUBJECTIVE: you approve the overall look and feel of the new <route> page
1385	
1386	````
1387	
1388	**Rules:**
1389	
1390	- The PR description is a **distillation**, not a copy. Do not paste PRD sections
1391	  verbatim.
1392	- "Why" must not contain solution language. If you catch yourself writing
1393	  "by adding X" or "through implementing Y", rewrite to focus on the problem.
1394	- "TLDR" is one sentence, 35 words or fewer, naming the user-visible outcome in the
1395	  surface the reader uses — no file, function, or line number — then what was wrong or
1396	  missing before and what is true now. On a fix-shaped PR it states the failure and the
1397	  causal resolution together.
1398	- "User-facing changes" and "System changes" bullets should each be testable against
1399	  the implementation. Avoid vague bullets like "improve the user experience".
1400	- "Key decisions" should only include decisions where a reasonable alternative
1401	  existed. Don't list obvious choices.
1402	- "User-facing changes" must be phrased in user terms (what someone running the
1403	  tool will see or do differently), not implementation terms, and names a surface
1404	  rather than a file, function, or line number.
1405	- "System changes" covers any internal change worth a reviewer's attention, and
1406	  prompts for ongoing cost (API calls, CI time, token spend) only when the change
1407	  moves one. It does NOT list file edits, helper refactors, or mechanical cleanups.
1408	- Both "User-facing changes" and "System changes" are mandatory: when the section is
1409	  empty, write the literal word `none` under the heading — never omit either heading
1410	  itself.
1411	- Always emit the `## Test Steps` heading, even for refactors. The auto-merge gate
1412	  treats a missing heading as an upstream regression and escalates `NEEDS HUMAN`.
1413	  Zero unchecked items under the heading is the auto-merge state; one or more
1414	  unchecked `- [ ]` items is the gate state.
1415	- Render every "Test Steps" entry as a `- [ ]` markdown checkbox so reviewers can
1416	  tick items off as they verify and the auto-merge gate can count them.
1417	- Do not hard-wrap prose at a fixed column width. Write each paragraph as a single
1418	  line and let the renderer wrap it. Hard wraps go ragged the moment a sentence
1419	  is edited and add no value on GitHub, which renders one long line as one
1420	  flowing paragraph.
1421	- Save the draft to the `pr-description-draft.md` absolute path the wrapper passed
1422	  you. Create the parent `.flow-tmp/` directory first with `mkdir -p` if it
1423	  doesn't already exist — `/flow-pipeline` worktrees pre-register the path in
1424	  `.git/info/exclude` so it stays untracked, and a stray write at the worktree
1425	  root would block the post-merge `git worktree remove` in `/flow-pipeline`
1426	  step 10.
1427	
1428	## 8. Persist the consolidated plan
1429	
1430	Write the full PRD + task breakdown + PR-description draft to the `plan.md`
1431	absolute path the wrapper passed you. Create the parent `.flow-tmp/` directory
1432	first with `mkdir -p` if it doesn't already exist. Single artifact, sections
1433	in this order:
1434	
1435	```markdown
1436	# PRD
1437	
1438	<the structured PRD from step 5>
1439	
1440	# Candidate follow-up issues
1441	
1442	<optional — only when discovery surfaced orthogonal ideas; see step 5's
1443	"Candidate follow-up issues" sub-section. Omit the heading entirely when
1444	empty>
1445	
1446	# Task breakdown
1447	
1448	<the ordered tasks + Skills Summary from step 6>
1449	
1450	# PR description draft
1451	
1452	<the TLDR / User-facing changes / System changes / Why / Key decisions /
1453	Test Steps from step 7>
1454	````
1455	
1456	This file is the predictable handoff for the `/flow-pipeline` supervisor — it
1457	reads `.flow-tmp/plan.md` after the wrapper returns to drive the implement phase.
1458	When `/flow-product-planning` is run manually (no supervisor), the same file is still
1459	useful as a single artifact the user can share or iterate on. Overwrite any prior
1460	`.flow-tmp/plan.md`; do not append.
1461	
1462	The path lives under `.flow-tmp/` (rather than the worktree root) so the
1463	post-merge `git worktree remove` in `/flow-pipeline` step 10 doesn't choke on a
1464	stray untracked file. `flow-new-worktree` registers the path in
1465	`.git/info/exclude`, and `flow-remove-worktree` cleans the directory before
1466	removing the worktree.
1467	
1468	The `pr-description-draft.md` write from step 7 is independent and stays — it's
1469	the artifact `pr-review` consumes. Both files should land.
1470	
1471	## 9. Return a brief summary
1472	
1473	Your final message back to the wrapper should be 4–6 labeled bullets:
1474	`Problem:` — the problem statement in one line; `Tasks:` — the number of
1475	tasks; `Candidates:` — the candidate follow-up issue count if non-zero
1476	(e.g. "3 candidate follow-up issues for the user to pick from"; omit the
1477	bullet when zero); `Top assumptions:` — the top one or two open questions
1478	or assumptions the user should pay attention to, listing any `**Needs user
1479	input:**` or `[confidence: low]` items first; `Research:` — **when
1480	Step 1.5's research path was active but no research ran, the one-line
1481	skip-note from (e)** (e.g. "Web-grounded research skipped — agy
1482	unavailable; force with `flow feature create --research`.") so it reaches
1483	chat; omit the bullet when research ran or the path was fully dormant;
1484	`Vetting verdict:` — (the `## Request vetting` `- **Verdict:**` line,
1485	verbatim). Do not paste the PRD or task list back — the wrapper only forwards your summary to the caller, and
1486	the artifacts on disk are the durable record. Keeping the return value
1487	short is the whole point of the subagent fan-out.
1488	
1489	**`Questions:` variant (question-gate fire).** When the `## Question-gate
1490	contract` above fired, replace the whole labeled-bullet summary with a
1491	single `Questions: <n> unresolved — see .flow-tmp/interview-questions.md`
1492	line (`<n>` is the frontier size written) instead of `Problem:` /
1493	`Tasks:` / etc. — there is no PRD to summarize on this path, and the
1494	wrapper reads the artifact-existence check (`## 3` "Suggest the next
1495	handoff") to route the pause per `/flow-pipeline` step 3's Question-gate
1496	branch.
1497	
1498	When the spawn prompt carries `REVISION: <n>`, **MUST Read `<SKILL_DIR>/references/discovery-revision.md` before step 1.**
1499	
1500	# Verification
1501	
1502	- PRD contains all sections (Problem, Scope Boundary, Stories, Architecture,
1503	  Constraints, Open Questions).
1504	- Every user story has testable acceptance criteria (not vague "works correctly").
1505	- Architecture Decisions section names specific layers, domain modules, and data
1506	  flow pattern.
1507	- Every assumption you made under ambiguity appears as an Open Question.
1508	- `[confidence: low]` items are counted at the question-gate mechanical floor
1509	  alongside unresolved `**Needs user input:**` items.
1510	- Task breakdown covers all PRD requirements with no gaps.
1511	- Each task has a recommended skill, inputs, outputs, and acceptance criteria.
1512	- Each task carries a `- **Contract:**` block (Files / Interfaces / Call-site
1513	  edits, or the change-type surgical form from the step-6 table), and its
1514	  acceptance criteria is a runnable command, not prose.
1515	- When ≥2 tasks have dependencies, the `| Task | Depends on |` dependency
1516	  table follows the task list.
1517	- Tasks are ordered by dependency (no task references an output that hasn't been
1518	  produced yet).
1519	- No task is too large for a single focused session (if it seems large, split it).
1520	- Skill recommendations reference skills that actually exist in the project's
1521	  skill directory.
1522	- PR description draft follows the standardized format (TLDR / User-facing
1523	  changes / System changes / Why / Key decisions / Test Steps), with both
1524	  `## User-facing changes` and `## System changes` always present — `none` when
1525	  empty — and the latter drawing Before/After pairs from the plan's
1526	  `### System flow` subsection when that subsection is non-`none`.
1527	- Both `.flow-tmp/plan.md` and `.flow-tmp/pr-description-draft.md` were written
1528	  at the absolute paths the wrapper passed you, with parent directory created on
1529	  demand.
1530	- `## Alternatives considered` is either omitted (no closed paths) or ≤3 one-line
1531	  entries with a concrete, verifiable rejection reason each; when present, a sibling
1532	  `.flow-tmp/excluded-paths.json` mirrors it 1:1.
1533	- `## Epic context` is either omitted (not epic-launched) or every claim in it traces
1534	  to a `design.md` / `manifest.json` read from step 1.7, and carries the Manifest
1535	  write-back line.
1536	- A failed premise check surfaces as a `**Premise check:**` line in the Problem
1537	  Statement and the `## Recommendation` verdict is non-`Proceed`; a sound premise
1538	  carries no line.
1539	- `flow-plan-lint` already checks the Goal line, the Problem Statement lead, the drafted PR TLDR, the drafted PR change bullets, Behavioral contrast, Recommendation, Plan risks, Cut list, Instrumentation, Runtime design (Recovery line, queue must-set settings), Request vetting, Existing-code assessment, Method selection, the Open Questions resolution / confidence / stakes markers, task Contract blocks, and the `excluded-paths.json` mirror, and `flow-candidate-issues --lint` already checks the candidate follow-up value bars, references, and bundling — do not re-verify those by hand.
1540	- **Self-check before returning:** run `flow-plan-lint --plan-md-file <the plan.md path>`
1541	  by bare PATH name and fix every named miss. Tolerant: when the helper is missing
1542	  from PATH, the check skips silently (same research-cache discipline as Step 1.5) —
1543	  never block on it. And
1544	  `flow-candidate-issues --lint --plan-md-file <the plan.md path>` (same tolerant
1545	  skip), fixing every `bundlingMisses` entry by bundling the item or naming its
1546	  exclusion.
1547	
1548	# Constraints
1549	
1550	- NEVER write application code — your sole output is strategy, the two artifact
1551	  files, and a brief return summary.
1552	- NEVER ask the user clarifying questions — the Task tool is one-shot. Make
1553	  informed assumptions and surface them as Open Questions.
1554	- NEVER hardcode the skill list — always read the skill directory to get the
1555	  current set.
1556	- NEVER skip loading `README.md` (or the project's primary architecture doc) —
1557	  your assumptions must be informed by existing architecture.
1558	- NEVER dump the full PRD into the PR description — distill problem, scope, and
1559	  decisions only.
1560	- NEVER paste the PRD or task list back to the wrapper as your return value —
1561	  the artifacts on disk are the record, the return summary is one short
1562	  paragraph.

1	<!-- Style: terse. Prefer structured markdown — tables and nested lists — over
2	     prose paragraphs unless prose is genuinely warranted; flow-shaped content
3	     (system/user flows, before → after comparisons) is never an arrow-paragraph.
4	     Cut prose that a heading + list could replace. Mermaid is at the planner's
5	     discretion, never required. Markdown is structure; structure is legibility. -->
6	
7	# [Feature Name]
8	
9	**Goal:** [one outcome-phrased sentence, ≤30 words, naming the observable result]
10	
11	<!-- Always present, directly under the title. Not a restatement of the title or
12	     request — names the outcome. Full contract: discovery-instructions.md "Goal line". -->
13	
14	## Problem Statement
15	
16	<!-- The pain, not the fix. Avoid "we need a button that…". Open with a
17	     plain-language lead of 2-4 sentences (no anchors, tables, lists, or internal
18	     identifiers) for a reader with no context: what the thing is for, what goes
19	     wrong or is missing today, and what that costs the reader. Evidence, tables,
20	     and anchors follow the lead. When the step-3 premise check fails, follow the
21	     lead with a **Premise check:** line naming what was assumed vs. what the
22	     codebase shows (omit-when-sound — no line when the premise holds), and set
23	     ## Recommendation to a non-Proceed verdict. -->

1	# Discovery runtime design procedure (read for every plan; the `none` form is cheap)
2	
3	This reference holds the discovery procedure for the always-present `### Runtime design` subsection of `## Architecture Decisions`: the trigger surface, the full form, the `none — <reason>` form, the required pre-reads and the task shape. `discovery-instructions.md` step 5 names it at the gate site.
4	
5	## Runtime defaults
6	
7	Apply these to every full-form plan. A plan that departs from one names the departure and its reason on the `**Proportionality:**` line.
8	
9	- Durable work (anything that must survive the response, or a loop of paid or rate-limited calls) is queue-driven, not run in the request.
10	- A scheduler tick only enqueues one task per unit; it never runs the units itself.
11	- Every outbound call has an explicit timeout.
12	- Queue consumers are idempotent under redelivery, keyed on business identity rather than a per-attempt random value.
13	- All paid-call spend goes through one cap or ledger at a single choke point.
14	
15	The interactive budget behind "run in the request" is 10 s, never the platform's request timeout.
16	
17	## Step 5 sub-sections
18	
19	### Runtime design
20	
21	**Gate: the plan touches a runtime surface.** The trigger surface is the same as Instrumentation's: a plan that adds or changes a request handler, a background job or queue consumer, an outbound API call, a multi-stage pipeline, or a connection or worker pool. Decide the form from the plan's Task breakdown:
22

confident guess. This is not ranked because it is not tradeable.

Then, in order. When two conflict, the higher one wins; the point of the
ranking is to decide those conflicts, not to rate importance in the abstract.

1. **User experience.** How the product feels to use: fewer interruptions,
   fewer things the user has to remember or re-check, fewer surprises. One
   notch below that, look and feel — the visible layout and polish of every
   surface the user reads.
2. **Cost.** Anything with financial implications — cloud and compute spend,
   and paid API calls. Prefer the cheaper path when the outcomes are
   comparable; anything that adds ongoing cost must say what it buys.
3. **Architecture and system design.** The shape of the system — its
   boundaries, its data flow, how it scales and performs, how it fails. A
   design decision is worth surfacing; the code that implements it is not.
4. **Product quality.** The product does what it says, predictably, and
   holds together as a whole — including degrading gracefully when an
   optional input is missing rather than failing hard.

## What "good" looks like

A reader who has **not** opened the code can act on the explanation. They can
tell what changed for the user, what it costs, what design choice was made
and why, and what to do next — without reading the diff, without meeting an
internal identifier, and without a second round-trip to ask what a sentence
meant.

## Non-goals

- Mechanism-first summaries — a diff restated as prose.
- Naming files, functions, or line numbers in anything the user reads,
  unless they asked for the technical version.
- Assuming the reader read the code, the diff, or the scrollback.
- Hedged, unfalsifiable claims ("should be fine", "looks right") standing in
  for a check something can actually fail.
- Growing surface area for its own sake: a new flag, config key, or file that
  no named reader consumes.

## Vocabulary

| Use                                                          | Avoid                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| what the user now sees, saves, or no longer has to do          | "refactored the internals"                        |
| the design choice and the alternative it beat                  | the module, file, or function that implements it  |
| "costs one extra call per run" / "adds ~N% to cloud spend"     | "negligible overhead"                             |
| "nothing is lost" / "what is lost is X"                        | "should be recoverable"                           |
| a named skip with its reason                                   | "failed" with no reason                           |
| plain nouns a reader already owns (plan, review, release)      | internal jargon a reader outside the team wouldn't recognize |

1	# Discovery Step 1.5 research procedure (read only when research fires)
2	
3	When `RESEARCH_ON` is `true` (or `FORCE_RESEARCH` is `true`), also resolve the four **optional budget overrides** from the same `.research` object before building the manifest in (c). Each is **tolerant by construction with one twist over the boolean read in discovery-instructions.md Step 1.5 (a)**: an absent key silently takes its v1 default; a key that is **present but the wrong JSON type emits a loud `stderr` warning and then falls back to the default** — it never throws and never aborts the pass (a config typo must degrade to a warning, mirroring the `allSkipped` graceful-skip discipline — research never blocks planning). A bare `// default` is **insufficient** because it only defaults on `null`/missing, not on a present wrong-type value, so each read type-guards explicitly:
4	
5	```bash
6	CFG=~/.flow/config.json
7	
8	# Tolerant per-key read. $1=key $2=expected-jq-type $3=default.
9	# absent -> silent default; present-but-wrong-type -> loud stderr warning + default;
10	# missing/malformed config file -> default. Never throws, never aborts.
11	read_budget() {
12	  local raw
13	  raw=$(jq -r "
14	    if (.research.$1) == null then \"__ABSENT__\"
15	    elif (.research.$1 | type) == \"$2\" then (.research.$1 | tostring)
16	    else \"__INVALID__\" end" "$CFG" 2>/dev/null) || raw="__ABSENT__"
17	  if [ "$raw" = "__ABSENT__" ] || [ -z "$raw" ]; then
18	    printf '%s' "$3"
19	  elif [ "$raw" = "__INVALID__" ]; then
20	    printf 'warn: research.%s is present but not a %s; using default %s\n' "$1" "$2" "$3" >&2
21	    printf '%s' "$3"
22	  else
23	    printf '%s' "$raw"
24	  fi
25	}
26	
27	RESEARCH_MAX_CALLS=$(read_budget maxCalls number 12)
28	RESEARCH_TIMEOUT=$(read_budget timeout string "20m")
29	RESEARCH_MODEL=$(read_budget model string "Gemini 4 Argon (High)")
30	RESEARCH_REFUTE_MODEL=$(read_budget refuteModel string "Claude Opus 5.5 (Medium)")
31	
32	# Cross-model diversity guard: the REFUTE entry MUST run on a DIFFERENT variant
33	# from GATHER (the adversarial check is worthless if both run the same model).
34	# If the resolved refute model collides with gather, warn and fall back to a
35	# pinned alternate that differs.
36	if [ "$RESEARCH_REFUTE_MODEL" = "$RESEARCH_MODEL" ]; then
37	  if [ "$RESEARCH_MODEL" = "Claude Opus 5.5 (Medium)" ]; then
38	    RESEARCH_REFUTE_MODEL="GPT-OSS 120B (Medium)"
39	  else
40	    RESEARCH_REFUTE_MODEL="Claude Opus 5.5 (Medium)"
41	  fi
42	  printf 'warn: research.refuteModel resolved equal to the gather model (%s); falling back refute to %s to preserve adversarial diversity\n' "$RESEARCH_MODEL" "$RESEARCH_REFUTE_MODEL" >&2

85	   ```bash
86	   PID=$(cat <out.json>.pid)
87	   flow-plan-review-wait <out.json> --complete-line --pid "$PID" --max-sec 540
88	   echo "elapsed: $(( $(date +%s) - $(cat <out.json>.start) ))s"
89	   ```
90	
91	   (`$RESEARCH_MAX_CALLS` defaults to `12`; `$RESEARCH_TIMEOUT` defaults to `20m`; `--concurrency` stays pinned at `4`.) The `rm -f` is load-bearing: a stale `<out.json>` from an earlier pass would satisfy the waiter instantly. The fan-out writes `--out` through a temp file and a rename and ends it with a newline, so `--complete-line` never sees a half-written aggregate. Re-run the wait call (it re-reads the saved pid) whenever it returns without a `"outcome":"complete"` line, until the file is complete, the process is gone (`"outcome":"process-exited-without-result"` — take the graceful skip in (e)), or the **give-up time** passes: one wave × the research limit + 5 minutes of slack, measured from the saved start time (the `elapsed:` line). On give-up, kill the fan-out's process group (`kill -- -"$(cat <out.json>.pid)"`; `$PID` is unset in a later Bash call) and take the graceful skip in (e) with reason `agy-unavailable` (the visibility note names the timeout in plain language).
92	
93	3. **The fan-out's own result is the agy-availability check — no separate probe.** If the aggregate is `allSkipped: true` (every entry `ran: false` with `skipReason: agy-not-found` / `agy-not-authenticated`), agy is unavailable: take the graceful skip in (e). Otherwise read the per-entry artifacts under `<out-dir>/artifacts/` and synthesize the report yourself (d). A non-`allSkipped` aggregate carrying any `ran: false` entry is folded into the plan as a named limitation (in plain language), never read as an absence of findings.
94	
95	**Budget is config-tunable within a HARD runtime ceiling:** `--max-calls` (the resolved `$RESEARCH_MAX_CALLS`, default `12`) is a real `flow-delegate-fanout` flag that hard-caps the total call count; the per-call timeout is the per-manifest-entry `timeout` field (the resolved `$RESEARCH_TIMEOUT`, default `"20m"`) you set on every entry. `--default-entry-timeout "$RESEARCH_TIMEOUT"` is the fanout-level **backstop** that HARD-enforces that per-call cap: any entry that omits its own `timeout` is dispatched with the resolved `$RESEARCH_TIMEOUT` instead of silently falling back to agy's 5-minute default. You SHOULD still set `timeout` on every manifest entry yourself — a per-entry `timeout` always wins over the flag, and being explicit keeps the manifest self-documenting; the flag is the safety net for when an entry forgets it. (Note: per-entry `--timeout` is **not** a `flow-delegate-fanout` flag — its parser rejects unknown flags — so the per-call cap lives only in the per-manifest-entry `timeout` field; `--default-entry-timeout` is the fanout-level default for that field, not a per-entry override.) An operator may override `maxCalls`, `timeout`, `model`, and `refuteModel` via `~/.flow/config.json` (resolved in (a)); `--concurrency` stays pinned at `4` and is **not** tunable, because it is load-bearing in the runtime-ceiling arithmetic below.
96	
97	_Runtime-ceiling rationale._ You are a **one-shot Task sub-agent with no yield/resume** and no wake-up notifications, so the detached fan-out is awaited by re-running the waiter in the foreground, in ≤ 9-minute steps — the run is never held inside one tool call, and the old "must finish inside ~10 minutes of sub-agent wall-clock" ceiling no longer bounds the research limit. The runtime is **one wave × the research limit, waited in ≤ 9-minute steps**: the three manifest entries fit one wave at `--concurrency 4`, so the worst case is `ceil(entries / concurrency) × timeout` = one `$RESEARCH_TIMEOUT` (20 minutes by default), and the give-up time adds 5 minutes of slack for the helper's own startup. The fan-out's own `--max-calls` still hard-caps the call count, and the per-entry `timeout` stays the load-bearing per-call cap (at agy's 5-minute default an entry could run shorter than a slow search needs). Evidence that sub-agents survive this: in the pipeline that raised the limit, two discovery sub-agents ran 16.5 and 9.6 minutes to completion. **Advisory (now that `maxCalls`/`timeout` are tunable):** raising `research.timeout` lengthens every pipeline that reaches this step by up to that much; keep it to what a gather actually needs (`flow-research-run`'s sizing rule in `docs/eval/argon-latency-probe/README.md`) — this is advisory, not enforced (there is no executable parser to validate it, by design).
98	
99	**(d) Synthesize, then fold a bounded, confidence-labeled findings summary into your prior context.** Read the fan-out's per-entry artifacts (the gather's cited findings + the refute's adversarial check, under `<out-dir>/artifacts/`). Each artifact is now a `--output-format json` envelope, not raw prose — before synthesizing, unwrap it: prefer `structured_output` when present, else `response`, else (only if the file fails to parse as JSON) fall back to the raw artifact text. Check `denied_actions` on each envelope too — a non-empty list means agy refused a tool and the entry may carry little or no usable content; fold that into the plan as a named limitation (see the fan-out-result step above), never silently read as "nothing was found." Once unwrapped, synthesize a confidence-ranked summary yourself, and fold a **bounded** version into your discovery reasoning — and, where load-bearing, surface a short **"Research findings (prior context)"** note in `plan.md`. Constraints on what enters the plan:
100	
101	- **Each finding carries its confidence label (high/medium/low) INTACT.** Never flatten the gathered confidence ranking into false certainty.
102	- **Refuted, contested, or low-confidence claims become RISKS or open questions — NEVER firm plan assumptions or decisions.** This is the uncertainty-laundering guard: a gathered-but-shaky claim must not become a load-bearing decision.
103	- **Never paste raw per-source artifacts or full-length quotes into `plan.md`.** Only the bounded summary — bound your own synthesis (top-N ranked claims, capped quotes, no raw pages), exactly as the `/flow-research` procedure you read prescribes.
104	
105	**Cache-write (after the synthesis is produced).** Persist the bounded synthesis so the next identical re-run (same-scope redirect / crash-resume) hits and skips the fan-out. Write the synthesis to a file and store it by **bare PATH name** under the SAME normalized sharp question used for the read in (c):
106	
107	```bash
108	flow-research-cache put --question "<the same sharp question from 1.5(b)>" --synthesis-file <synthesis-file>
109	```
110	
111	(or pipe the synthesis via `--synthesis -`). This is a no-op on the cache-hit path — you only reach (d) on a miss. The `put` is best-effort: a write failure must not error discovery.

1:# Discovery Playbook
6:## Conversational Techniques
8:### Ladder Up (Solution → Problem)
16:### Ladder Down (Problem → Scenario)
24:### Fork (Vague → Two Options)

1	---
2	name: flow-system-design
3	description: >-
4	  Choose execution model, timeouts, retries, idempotency and cost caps for new
5	  runtime work. TRIGGER on "add a background job", "this takes minutes", "add a
6	  webhook", "schedule a refresh", "make this reliable", or a change adding a
7	  handler, job, queue consumer or outbound call. SKIP metrics/alerts
8	  (flow-metrics), client loading states (flow-ui-ux), Postgres mechanics
9	  (supabase-postgres-best-practices).
10	---
11	
12	# Goal
13	
14	Make every new piece of runtime work survive real traffic, retries and a bad day without the owner asking. A slow, paid or periodic operation built as "just run it in the handler" loses work on a deploy, double-charges on a retry and has no ceiling on spend, and nobody notices until the bill or the support queue says so. This skill fixes the questions once: who waits, how long it can take, what happens when it runs twice, what stops it from running away, and what the owner sees when it fails. It is equally a guard against over-building, so a fast call stays a plain function call.
15	
16	# When to Use
17	
18	- A plan or change adds a request handler, background job, queue consumer, scheduled task, webhook, or an outbound call to a paid or rate-limited service.
19	- A request says "add a background job", "this takes minutes", "add a webhook", "schedule a refresh", or "make this reliable".
20	- `/flow-new-feature` lists this skill's paths in an edit-set entry's `skill_docs` because the plan's `### Runtime design` is not `none`.
21	- A review finding names work continuing after the response, a missing timeout, unbounded retries, or an unguarded paid call.
22	
23	# When NOT to Use
24	
25	- Metrics, dashboards, alerts and SLOs — defer to `flow-metrics` (step 9 only points there).
26	- Client-side loading and progress states — defer to `flow-ui-ux`.
27	- Postgres mechanics (indexes, locking, pooling, queries) — defer to `supabase-postgres-best-practices` when installed; architecture-level data rules are in `references/data.md`.
28	- Docs-only, style-only or behaviour-preserving refactors: the plan carries `### Runtime design` = `none — <reason>` and nothing changes.
29	- Pre-launch scale work (sharding, multi-region, autoscaling tuning). Name it in the Proportionality pass and leave it out.
30	
31	# Context
32	
33	Read only what applies. Each line says when:
34	
35	- [GCP mapping](references/gcp.md): GCP repos. Cloud Run, Cloud Tasks, Pub/Sub, Scheduler, Jobs and budgets, with their ceilings.
36	- [Cloudflare mapping](references/cloudflare.md): Cloudflare Workers repos. Workers, Queues, Cron Triggers, Workflows, Durable Objects, KV and D1, with their ceilings.
37	- [AWS mapping](references/aws.md): AWS repos. API Gateway, Lambda, SQS, EventBridge Scheduler, Step Functions and Budgets, with their ceilings.
38	- [Data patterns](references/data.md): the change persists state. Outbox, idempotency keys, claim/lease rows, enqueue-after-commit, expand/contract, retention, one spend ledger.
39	- [Multi-step work](references/workflows.md): one request starts several steps or sections. Parent/child rows, fan-in, checkpointing, compensation, when to use a workflow engine.
40	- [Rollout and rollback](references/rollout.md): the change alters a schema, a queue payload, a public API or a paid path. Reversible deploys, versioned payloads, canaries, flags.
41	- [Caching](references/caching.md): the same expensive or paid result is read repeatedly. Cache-aside, TTLs, stampedes, CDN versus shared cache.
42	- [Backup and recovery](references/recovery.md): the change adds a datastore, stores irreplaceable data, or deletes in bulk. RPO/RTO, PITR, restore drills.
43	- [Progress and real-time updates](references/realtime.md): a client watches queued work or a stream. Polling, SSE, WebSockets, reconnects.
44	- [API contracts](references/api.md): the change adds or alters an endpoint or webhook receiver. 202 + status, idempotency keys, errors, rate limits, pagination, versioning.
45	
46	The principles below are the portable core; each cites its authority:
47	
48	- Processes are disposable and must tolerate being stopped at any moment, so work that must not be lost cannot live only in memory ([12-factor disposability](https://12factor.net/disposability)).
49	- Every outbound call needs a timeout, and retries need capped exponential backoff with jitter ([AWS Builders' Library: timeouts, retries and backoff](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)).
50	- Retries are only safe when the operation is idempotent ([AWS: making retries safe with idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/); [Stripe on idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)).
51	- Retrying at several layers multiplies load and turns a blip into an outage ([SRE book: cascading failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)).
52	- Under overload, shed or cap work deliberately instead of queueing without bound ([SRE book: handling overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)).
53	- Reliability is a design input, not a later hardening pass ([Google Cloud reliability pillar](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability); [AWS reliability pillar](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/welcome.html)).
54	- Users lose the sense of an instant response past about 0.1 s, their flow of thought past about 1 s, and their attention past about 10 s, which is why the interactive budget defaults to 10 s ([NN/g: response times](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/)).
55	- Build only what today's requirement needs ([Fowler: YAGNI](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/Yagni.html)).
56	
57	# Instructions
58	
59	## 1. Read the platform and reuse what exists
60	
61	Find the repo's platform (deploy config, Dockerfile, wrangler or terraform files) and its existing primitives: a queue, a retry helper, a spend ledger, an idempotency table. Reuse them before adding a second one.
62	
63	## 2. Classify each operation
64	
65	For every operation the change adds, note: who waits for the result, an estimated p99, its side effects, its cost per call, and what triggers it (request, schedule, event).
66	
67	## 3. Pick the execution model
68	
69	The test is whether losing the work is acceptable, not whether it is async. The interactive budget is 10 s. It is never the platform's request timeout: a 300 s Cloud Run limit means the request is killed at 300 s, not that a user will wait that long. Pick from this table:
70	
71	| Situation                                                                                                                                                                                    | Execution model                                                                                                                                |
72	| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
73	| Caller waits, p99 under the interactive budget, no paid or rate-limited call loop                                                                                                            | inline, with a timeout on every outbound call                                                                                                  |
74	| Caller waits on a bounded set of paid calls whose aggregate p99 is under the interactive budget                                                                                              | inline, with a timeout and the repo's spend cap at the call site                                                                               |
75	| Work whose loss is not acceptable and that outlives the request, runs over the interactive budget, loops over paid or rate-limited calls with unbounded or variable cardinality, or fans out | durable queue + worker invoked synchronously under the queue's attempt deadline; respond 202 + a status resource                               |
76	| Model generation whose result is persisted, even when it would fit inside the request timeout or is streamed to a watching user                                                              | queue; the client reads progress from the status resource                                                                                      |
77	| Multi-step or multi-section work (a report with several generated sections)                                                                                                                  | one queued task per step plus a parent status row ([workflows](references/workflows.md))                                                       |
78	| Best-effort post-response work whose loss is acceptable (telemetry beacon, cache warm)                                                                                                       | the platform's bounded post-response hook (e.g. Cloudflare `waitUntil`) with an explicit timeout; never for generation or billing side effects |
79	| Periodic work                                                                                                                                                                                | the scheduler tick only enqueues one task per unit; it never runs the units itself                                                             |
80	| One unit exceeds the queue attempt ceiling                                                                                                                                                   | batch job, or split into checkpointed steps                                                                                                    |
81	| Never                                                                                                                                                                                        | work that must not be lost continuing after the response, in-memory queues, timers as job runners                                              |
82	
83	## 4. Make repeats safe
84	
85	Derive an idempotency key from business identity (not a random value minted per attempt). Dedupe at the consumer and record the key atomically with the side effect (`references/data.md`).
86	
87	## 5. Bound every wait
88	
89	Put a timeout on every outbound call. Deadlines shrink inward: the handler's deadline is smaller than the queue's, and each call's is smaller than the handler's.
90	
91	## 6. Retry at one layer
92	
93	Retry at exactly one layer, with capped exponential backoff, jitter and bounded attempts. Classify failures as permanent (stop, mark failed) or transient (retry).
94	
95	## 7. Bound the cost
96	
97	Enforce a cost bound at one choke point, reusing the repo's spend ledger when it has one. A per-call counter scattered across call sites does not add up to a cap.
98	
99	## 8. Cap overload
100	
101	Set concurrency limits, queue rate caps and, where the caller is anonymous, per-caller limits or load shedding, so a spike cannot become unbounded spend or a self-inflicted outage.
102	
103	## 9. Observability
104	
105	Defer to `flow-metrics` for metrics, dashboards and alerts. Here, only make sure each operation has a place to emit them.
106	
107	## 10. Show failure
108	
109	A failed unit lands in a visible failed state (a status field, a dead-letter destination) that an owner or user can see and re-drive. Never swallow it.
110	
111	## 11. Proportionality pass
112	
113	Name what was deliberately left out and why: no queue for a 50 ms call, no sharding or multi-region before launch, no dead-letter topic for a job nobody would replay. Write it on the plan's `**Proportionality:**` line.
114	
115	## 12. Record the design in the plan
116	
117	The plan's `### Runtime design` section (under `## Architecture Decisions`) carries one table:
118	
119	| Operation | Est. p99 | Execution model | Timeout / deadline | Retries | Idempotency key | Cost bound |
120	| --------- | -------- | --------------- | ------------------ | ------- | --------------- | ---------- |
121	
122	- An inline row may compress to `inline — <p99>, timeout <n>`.
123	- A cell that reuses a repo primitive names it in plain words, or `new`; the touching task lists its repo-relative path under `**Inputs:**` (`new: <path>` for a new one).
124	- A `**Platform:**` line (`gcp | cloudflare | aws | other`) and a `**Proportionality:**` line follow the table.
125	- A change with no runtime surface writes `none — <reason>` instead.
126	
127	# Anti-Patterns
128	
129	- Work that must not be lost continuing after the response returns (detached promise, timer, in-memory queue) on a platform that bills or freezes by request.
130	- A scheduler tick that does the work itself instead of enqueuing one task per unit.
131	- Piecemeal spend counters at each call site instead of one ledger and one choke point.
132	- Retries stacked at two layers (client, worker and queue each retrying).
133	- A queue, worker and status table for a 50 ms call.
134	- An idempotency key minted per attempt, which dedupes nothing.
135	- A worker or webhook endpoint that runs paid or side-effecting work without authenticating its caller.
136	
137	# Verification
138	
139	- Every operation in the change has a row (or an inline line) in `### Runtime design` with an execution model chosen by the table above.
140	- Every outbound call has a timeout; deadlines shrink inward.
141	- Retries live at one layer and are capped; the consumer dedupes on a business-identity key.
142	- Paid work is bounded at one choke point, and its failures reach a visible failed state.
143	- The Proportionality line names at least one thing deliberately left out, or says nothing was over-built.
144	
145	# Constraints
146	
147	- NEVER add a queue, worker or status resource to work that fits the inline row of the table.
148	- NEVER run periodic units inside the scheduler tick.
149	- NEVER let work that must not be lost continue after the response.
150	- NEVER import from flow's `bin/lib` when running in a consumer worktree; resolve skill paths with `flow-module-status --skill-path flow-system-design`.
151	- Stay vendor-neutral in the instructions: platform specifics live in `references/` only.
152

1	---
2	name: flow-metrics
3	description: >-
4	  Add custom application metrics, dashboards, alerts and SLOs. TRIGGER on
5	  "add metrics", "instrument this", "add a dashboard", "set up alerts", "define
6	  an SLO", or a change that adds or alters a request handler, background job,
7	  outbound API call, or multi-stage pipeline. SKIP logging and tracing; writing
8	  the tests goes to flow-testing; execution model, retries, idempotency, cost
9	  caps go to flow-system-design.
10	---
11	
12	# Goal
13	
14	Make every runtime change ship with consistent, low-cardinality custom metrics plus a dashboard, alert and SLO spec, without the owner asking. The owner reads an app's health from graphs, so a handler or job with no latency, volume or failure numbers is invisible until a user complains, and metric names or error labels that differ between changes make the graphs refuse to line up. This skill fixes the vocabulary once per repo: OpenTelemetry names, one closed `error.type` list, one attribute registry, a cardinality budget, and a per-backend translation.
15	
16	# When to Use
17	
18	- A plan or change adds or alters a request handler, a background job or queue consumer, an outbound API call, a multi-stage pipeline, or a connection or worker pool.
19	- A request says "add metrics", "instrument this", "what should we measure", "add a dashboard", "set up alerts", or "define an SLO".
20	- `/flow-new-feature` lists this skill's paths in an edit-set entry's `skill_docs` because the plan's `## Instrumentation` section is not `none`.
21	- A review finding names unbounded metric labels, an `error.type` missing from `.flow/metrics.md`, or a runtime change with no emission.
22	
23	# When NOT to Use
24	
25	- Logging and distributed tracing — out of scope; this skill covers metrics, dashboards, alerts and SLOs only.
26	- Writing the tests themselves beyond the emission recipe — defer to `flow-testing`.
27	- Hand-writing HTTP-edge request metrics that auto-instrumentation already emits (see Instructions step 3).
28	- Docs-only, style-only or behaviour-preserving refactor changes: the plan carries a `none — <reason>` line and nothing is instrumented.
29	- Bootstrapping a metrics backend or a Grafana stack. With no backend, record `none yet` and stop there.
30	
31	# Context
32	
33	Load the relevant reference on demand — do not read all of them up front:
34	
35	- `.flow/metrics.md` in the target repo — the repo's committed metrics contract. Read it as REQUIRED context when it exists; it is authoritative over the starter values in the references.
36	- [Conventions](references/conventions.md) — OpenTelemetry naming, instruments, saturation and backlog signals, bounded-but-large dimensions, the closed `error.type` rule, the attribute registry, the cardinality budget, per-stage timing, the emission-test recipe.
37	- [Backends](references/backends.md) — the OpenTelemetry to Prometheus, Datadog, Workers Analytics Engine and Google Cloud Monitoring mapping (levels included), detection signals, the helper's per-backend adapter shape and test recipe.
38	- [Dashboards, alerts and SLOs](references/dashboards-alerts-slos.md) — the panel spec, SLI/SLO spec, burn-rate and saturation alerts, dashboard links, and the as-code rule.
39	
40	# Instructions
41	
42	## 1. Read the repo's contract
43	
44	Read `.flow/metrics.md` when it exists. When it does not, detect the backend, any dashboard or alert config, and any auto-instrumentation using the detection signals in `references/backends.md`. Absent is a legitimate state: the first instrumented change creates the file.
45	
46	## 2. Create or reuse the repo-local metrics helper
47	
48	On the first instrumented change, create one repo-local metrics helper — for example `instrument(op, fn)` and `recordStage(op, stage, fn)` — with a closed `ErrorType` union that mirrors `.flow/metrics.md` (`_OTHER` included) behind a swappable recorder. Type the attributes as one map from each registered key to its closed value union, mirroring `.flow/metrics.md` `## Attributes`. Add level and delta recording when the repo first needs a custom gauge or up-down counter, and track an in-flight count inside `instrument(op, fn)`'s `try`/`finally`. The backend adapter lives only there; with no backend it is a zero-dependency in-memory recorder. Later changes call the helper and never touch a backend client directly, so an unlisted `error.type` or an unregistered attribute fails the repo's own typecheck. Record its path under `## Helper` in `.flow/metrics.md`.
49	
50	## 3. Choose what to measure
51	
52	For each trigger surface in the change, record:
53	
54	- One duration histogram per operation, in seconds, split by `operation.outcome` (`ok` | `error`), plus only the keys the instruments table in `references/conventions.md` allows for it.
55	- One failures counter per operation, split by `error.type`.
56	- A per-stage histogram with a closed `operation.stage` attribute for multi-stage operations.
57	- One outbound-call histogram per dependency, split by `server.address` and `operation.outcome`.
58	- Saturation signals for queue consumers, jobs and pools: backlog and oldest-message age, in-flight count, pool usage. Take the platform-native metric first and emit a custom one only where it is blind (`references/conventions.md`).
59	
60	Never duplicate a metric that auto-instrumentation already emits. Put custom metrics where it is blind: stages, outbound calls, jobs, and domain failures behind a successful response.
61	
62	## 4. Map every failure to the closed `error.type` list
63	
64	Map each failure to a value from the repo's closed `error.type` list at one choke point (the helper), with `_OTHER` as the fallback. Never use raw messages, IDs or raw URL paths as a label value. When a genuinely new failure class appears, extend the list in `.flow/metrics.md` and the helper's union in the same change. Rename or redefine an existing value only in the same change that updates every dashboard query and alert reading it.
65	
66	## 5. Apply the cardinality budget
67	
68	State the estimated series total per operation and, on a per-sample backend, samples per month (the formula is in `references/conventions.md`) and justify anything over 100. Route templates, never raw paths. A large dimension is allowed only when its value set is fixed by code or product (`references/conventions.md`, bounded-but-large dimensions).
69	
70	## 6. Translate names per backend
71	
72	Translate the OpenTelemetry names for the repo's backend using `references/backends.md`: read the mapping table and only the section for the repo's `## Backend`, so a repo on one backend does not load another's detail. Do not change the semantics: unit in seconds, `operation.outcome`-split histogram, `error.type` on the failures counter and never on a histogram.
73	
74	## 7. Spec the dashboard, alert and SLO
75	
76	Extend the panel spec and name the SLO each operation rolls into using `references/dashboards-alerts-slos.md`. Add a new SLO only for a new user journey. Write dashboard or alert config as code only where the repo already keeps it; otherwise the spec lives in `.flow/metrics.md`. Dashboard links are static and stay behind login, never public share links (`references/dashboards-alerts-slos.md`).
77	
78	## 8. Add emission tests
79	
80	Against the helper's in-memory recorder, add one success test, one failure test per new `error.type` branch, a test that stage timings are recorded, and a gauge or in-flight test where the change adds one. Use the per-backend recipe in `references/backends.md` when the backend has no in-memory exporter.
81	
82	## 9. Create or extend `.flow/metrics.md`
83	
84	Create the file on the first instrumented change and extend it afterwards. Its shape:
85	
86	- `## Backend` — library and exporter, or `none yet — suggested: <x>`. With no backend, name the stack's natural default: Workers Analytics Engine on Cloudflare, Google Cloud Monitoring on GCP, the OpenTelemetry SDK elsewhere. On Google Cloud, also record the ingestion route (Cloud Monitoring exporter, or OTLP / Managed Prometheus) and how it stores a dotted key; the routes and the default rule are in `references/backends.md`.
87	- `## Namespace` — the metric name prefix.
88	- `## Attributes` — table: key | closed values or source | metrics | meaning, plus a `slot` column on Workers Analytics Engine.
89	- `## error.type values` — table: value | meaning | example cause.
90	- `## Helper` — path of the repo-local metrics helper.
91	- `## Dashboard panels` — the repo's one accumulating panel table.
92	- `## Dashboards` — table: name | URL | what it answers.
93	- `## Alerts` — burn-rate tiers plus saturation threshold rows, defined once; each row carries a `page` or `notify` action, the channel it routes to (a name, never a webhook URL or key) and a dashboard link.
94	- `## As-code` — paths of dashboard or alert files the repo keeps, or `spec-only`.
95	- `## SLOs` — few, journey-based.
96	- `## Coverage` — the operations instrumented so far, extended by each change, so a quiet graph is never mistaken for an unmeasured path.
97	
98	Every table keeps one row per value, sorted by its first column, so parallel changes append without merge conflicts. Never put secrets in the file.
99	
100	The change that records the first dashboard URL also adds a one-line "Observability" entry to the repo README linking the overview dashboard and `.flow/metrics.md`.
101	
102	With `backend: none yet`, only the PR that creates `.flow/metrics.md` carries the full note that graphs need a backend choice; later PRs carry one line saying these metrics are recorded but won't show on any graph until a metrics backend is chosen (status in `.flow/metrics.md` `## Backend`).
103	
104	# Anti-Patterns
105	
106	- A raw error message, exception text, user or request ID, or raw URL path used as a label value — it multiplies series without bound and the monitoring bill with it.
107	- A second error list in a plan or a handler instead of extending `.flow/metrics.md`.
108	- Recording a metric straight against a backend client in a handler instead of through the repo's helper.
109	- `error.type` on the duration histogram: it multiplies every error value by the bucket count. Use the `operation.outcome` split plus the failures counter.
110	- Separate success and failure counters with no histogram: latency percentiles are lost.
111	- Durations recorded in milliseconds under a seconds unit.
112	- Averaging percentiles on a dashboard instead of reading them from histograms.
113	- A new SLO per change instead of rolling into an existing journey SLO.
114	- A synonym of a registered attribute key instead of reusing it.
115	- A per-entity ID (tenant, user) as a label on a series-billed backend or Google Cloud Monitoring.
116	- A `rate()` over a gauge.
117	- A utilisation ratio emitted as a gauge; a ratio cannot be summed across instances.
118	- An alert that opens a ticket instead of paging or notifying.
119	- A public dashboard share link.
120	
121	# Verification
122	
123	- `.flow/metrics.md` exists and lists every operation the change instruments under `## Coverage`.
124	- Every metric follows the naming and unit rules in `references/conventions.md`, every attribute key is listed in `## Attributes`, and every attribute value comes from a closed set.
125	- Each new operation states its estimated series total (and samples per month on a per-sample backend).
126	- Saturation signals for each queue consumer or pool are specced, or named as platform-native.
127	- Every alert row names a channel and a dashboard link.
128	- Emission tests cover one success, one failure per new `error.type` branch, and stage timings.
129	- Dashboard config was touched only where the repo already keeps it; the panels and SLO are named either way.
130	- No metric duplicates what auto-instrumentation already emits.
131	
132	# Constraints
133	
134	- NEVER emit a raw message, ID or raw URL path as a metric label.
135	- NEVER bootstrap a metrics backend, a Prometheus or Grafana stack, or generate dashboard or alert files in a repo that does not already keep them.
136	- NEVER add a merge-blocking metrics gate; this skill guides and the review lens flags, nothing fails a commit.
137	- NEVER import from flow's `bin/lib` when running in a consumer worktree; resolve skill paths with `flow-module-status --skill-path flow-metrics`.
138	- Stay vendor-neutral in the instructions: backend specifics live in `references/backends.md` only.

# Progress and real-time updates

Read this when a client needs to see progress of queued work, a streamed model response, or updates pushed by other users.

## Pick the lightest channel

| Need                                                             | Channel                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Progress of a queued job, updates every few seconds are fine     | poll the status resource with backoff (start ~1 s, cap ~10 s); stop on a terminal status                                                                                        |
| Server-to-client stream (tokens of a model response, job events) | Server-Sent Events: one HTTP response, auto-reconnect, works through most proxies. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events |
| Two-way, low-latency (collaboration, presence, chat)             | WebSockets: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455                                                                                                                              |
| Many subscribers to shared state                                 | a managed realtime service (Supabase Realtime, Firebase, Cloudflare Durable Objects) rather than hand-built fan-out                                                             |

## Rules

- The durable status row is the source of truth; the live channel is a convenience. A client that disconnects reconnects and reads the row, so nothing depends on holding a connection open.
- Streaming a model response to a watching user does not make the generation inline: the generation runs in the worker and writes chunks or progress to storage, and the stream reads from there. A closed tab must not cancel or lose paid work.
- Give every stream event an id so a reconnecting client resumes with `Last-Event-ID` instead of replaying from the start.
- Long-lived connections count against platform limits: Cloud Run caps a request (including a WebSocket or SSE stream) at the service's request timeout, at most 60 minutes, so clients must reconnect. https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/triggering/websockets
- Authenticate the channel the same way as the status resource, and scope subscriptions to what the user may read.

## Proportionality

Polling a status endpoint is enough for jobs that take tens of seconds or more. Add SSE when users watch tokens arrive; add WebSockets only for genuinely two-way interaction.

# Google Cloud mapping

Read this on repos deployed to Google Cloud. It maps each principle in `../SKILL.md` to the service that implements it and states the ceilings that change the design. Every ceiling cites its Google doc and was retrieved on 2026-11-03; re-check a number before building something that sits close to it.

## Cloud Run services

- Request-based billing allocates CPU only while a request is being processed, so work continuing after the response is throttled or frozen. This is why the SKILL.md table forbids post-response continuation. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/billing-settings
- The request timeout defaults to 5 minutes and can be raised to at most 60 minutes. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/request-timeout
- On shutdown the container receives SIGTERM and has a 10 second period before SIGKILL, so in-flight work must be resumable. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/container-contract
- Set a maximum instance count and a per-instance concurrency on any service that calls a paid API: they are the overload cap in step 8.

## Cloud Tasks

- The default dispatch deadline for an HTTP target handler is 10 minutes, with a maximum of 30 minutes. Keep the worker's own timeout below it. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/creating-http-target-tasks
- A named task is deduplicated on its name, which is the natural place for the business-identity key. Deduplication is not instant: a name can stay reserved after the task finishes, so do not rely on it alone; also dedupe at the consumer. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/creating-http-target-tasks
- Queue retry config sets max attempts, min and max backoff, and max doublings; rate and concurrency caps (`maxDispatchesPerSecond`, `maxConcurrentDispatches`) throttle the worker. Retry here and nowhere else. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/configuring-queues
- Must-set settings: the dispatch deadline and max attempts belong in the task that creates the queue; flow-plan-lint checks the Task breakdown for them.
- Give the HTTP target an OIDC token (`oidcToken.serviceAccountEmail`) and accept only that caller: deploy the worker as its own Cloud Run service with `--no-allow-unauthenticated` and grant the queue's service account `roles/run.invoker`, or verify the token's audience and email in the handler. A worker route on a public service lets anyone trigger paid work and skip the queue's rate and spend caps.
- A handler that responds 2xx within the deadline completes the task; any other response retries it. This is the "worker invoked synchronously under the attempt deadline" shape.

## Pub/Sub

- Use for fan-out events with several independent subscribers. For one worker doing one job per unit, Cloud Tasks gives more control (named dedupe, rate caps).
- A subscription's acknowledgment deadline is 10 seconds by default, with a maximum of 600 seconds. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscription-properties
- Use an authenticated push subscription (OIDC token from a service account) and accept only that caller on the worker endpoint; an open push endpoint lets anyone trigger paid work.
- Attach a dead-letter topic with a bounded delivery-attempt count so a poison message becomes a visible failed state. The maximum push-endpoint response time beyond that ack deadline is unverified; check the page above before relying on it.
- Must-set settings: the ack deadline and a dead-letter topic belong in the task that creates the subscription; flow-plan-lint checks the Task breakdown for them.

## Cloud Scheduler

- A scheduler job is a clock, not a worker: its tick enqueues one Cloud Tasks task per unit (or publishes one event) and returns. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs/schedule-run-cron-job
- Authenticate the target with OIDC (a service account), never a shared secret in the URL.

## Cloud Run Jobs

- Each task defaults to a 10 minute maximum; the maximum task timeout is 168 hours (7 days). Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/task-timeout
- Use for a single unit that exceeds the Cloud Tasks 30 minute ceiling, or for batch work. Tasks can be sharded across parallel containers; each shard still needs its own idempotency key and checkpoint.

## Secret Manager

- Keep API keys and signing secrets here and mount or fetch them at start; never bake them into the image or the task payload.

## Billing budgets

- An alerts-only budget does not cap usage or spending; it only notifies. Spend-cap budgets exist only for supported services. An application-level cap (the single spend ledger in `data.md`) is still required. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets

## Monitoring

Defer to `flow-metrics`, which owns the Google Cloud Monitoring mapping. Platform-native backlog and oldest-task age for Cloud Tasks and Pub/Sub already exist; use them before adding custom gauges.
